strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: reducing reliance on large annotated datasets for anatomical understanding in medical imaging by using a single annotated reference image plus VLM-driven spatial reasoning.

The three-stage pipeline (VQA labeling -> bbox prediction with optimal-transport global matching -> VLM+SAM2 fused segmentation) is a sensible progression, and the paper provides a reasonably thorough empirical narrative showing why each stage motivates the next (e.g., VQA struggling with dense targets, bboxes failing for elongated vessels).

Evaluation spans two in-distribution and multiple out-of-distribution datasets across diverse modalities (CT, X-ray angiography, ultrasound, skeletal radiographs), which is a positive practice for assessing generalization in medical imaging applications.

The ablation on VLM initialization (Vanilla vs SFT-VQA vs RL-VQA) provides some insight into why RL-based pretraining of the VLM component benefits the downstream SAM2-integrated pipeline, particularly for OOD robustness.
Qualitative figures (main paper and appendix) illustrate concrete failure/success cases (e.g., mirrored reference image, vessel branch continuity) that help contextualize the quantitative gains.
weaknesses: Serious citation/attribution integrity concerns: several references appear to be mismatched or possibly fabricated/hallucinated (e.g., 'Balibar & Walsh, 2006' cited for GLIP is actually a biochemistry paper on gliotoxin synthesis; 'Pyatt, 1988' cited for SAM is an economics paper on Social Accounting Matrices, unrelated to Segment Anything; 'Nasser & Chen, 2007' cited for SEEM is a wireless sensor network routing paper, not the referenced vision-language segmentation model). This is a significant credibility issue that undermines trust in scholarly rigor, especially given the paper explicitly disclaims LLM-generated content in ideas/writing.

Reported metrics in Tables 2-4 are described as 'best score' across training steps/epochs without a clear held-out validation protocol; this raises concern about implicit test-set-based model selection, which can inflate reported numbers and complicate fair comparison across baselines.

No comparison against strong existing segmentation baselines mentioned in Related Work (e.g., MedSAM, TotalSegmentator, nnU-Net) is quantitatively included in the main results tables; only a brief qualitative mention that segmentation quality 'does not yet match a fully specialized nnU-Net' without numbers.

The DINOv2-based reference retrieval module (Fig. 2a), which selects the matched template from a reference bank, is not evaluated in isolation — there is no ablation quantifying retrieval accuracy or its effect on downstream performance, despite being a critical component of the pipeline for practical deployment beyond fixed reference-target pairs.

Several technical/writing issues remain unresolved (e.g., 'Z,000 extremity images' placeholder-like typo in Appendix A.2 dataset description for LERA), suggesting incomplete proofreading that also raises reliability concerns about other reported dataset statistics and numbers.

The core technical novelty is largely a combination of existing components (SFT+GRPO fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-VL, SAM2 memory-based segmentation, optimal transport matching) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the paper would benefit from clearer articulation of what specifically is new versus adapted from prior work (e.g., LISA's <SEG> token mechanism is conceptually very similar to the <Seg> token design used here).

Variance/robustness of results is not reported (no standard deviation across seeds or runs), making it hard to assess whether reported gains are statistically meaningful, particularly given relatively small OOD test sets (e.g., CAMUS, LERA).

strengths: Addresses a clinically relevant and underexplored problem: leveraging a single annotated reference image to guide VLM-based anatomical understanding without large-scale per-task annotation, which is well motivated by the data scarcity in medical imaging.

The three-stage progression (VQA -> bbox prediction with optimal-transport global matching -> VLM+SAM2 fusion) is a coherent narrative that clearly motivates why coarser localization schemes are insufficient for thin/elongated anatomical structures (e.g., vessels), and each stage is empirically justified.

The core technical idea of projecting VLM <Seg> token embeddings into SAM2's memory-bank space via attention is a reasonable and relatively lightweight way to combine language-grounded spatial reasoning with SAM2's fine-grained segmentation and its native memory mechanism.

Fairly extensive empirical evaluation across 2 in-distribution and 2-4 out-of-distribution datasets spanning diverse modalities (CT, X-ray angiography, bone X-ray, cardiac ultrasound), with consistent gains over SAM2-based memory baselines in both Dice and gIoU, and good qualitative examples showing topology preservation on elongated structures.

The ablation on VLM initialization (Vanilla vs SFT vs RL) is informative and supports the claim that RL-based fine-tuning yields better OOD generalization than pure SFT, which is a useful practical finding.

Reasonable comparisons against existing medical VLM baselines (Med-VLM-R1, MedFlamingo) that contextualize why naive application of RL/few-shot learning is insufficient and motivate the proposed reference-based relational reasoning strategy.
weaknesses: The reference list contains numerous clearly mismatched citations (e.g., 'GLIP' cited to an unrelated biochemistry paper on gliotoxin synthesis, 'SEEM' cited to a wireless sensor network routing protocol paper, 'OWL-ViT' cited to a roadway-asset detection paper, 'SAM' cited to a 1988 economic policy-modeling paper, 'DINO' conflated across unrelated works). This is a serious attribution/quality issue that undermines confidence in the rigor of the writing process, despite the paper's LLM usage statement disclaiming AI-generated content.
Placeholder/typo artifacts remain in the text (e.g., 'approximately Z,000 extremity images' in the LERA dataset description), suggesting insufficient proofreading.

The primary segmentation baselines (SAM2-Memory, SAM2-Memory-Ref-SFT) are relatively weak reference points; comparisons to other stronger few-shot/one-shot medical segmentation approaches (e.g., retrieval-augmented segmentation, other referring-segmentation VLM+SAM pipelines like LISA/EVF-SAM adapted to medical images) are largely missing, making it harder to assess RAU's relative standing against the current state of the art in reference-based segmentation.

No variance/error bars or statistical significance testing is reported for the main results, and dataset sizes for some OOD sets (e.g., LERA) are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility assessment.

The method still depends on a curated reference bank with DINOv2-based template retrieval; the sensitivity of final performance to reference bank quality, size, or mismatch between reference and target anatomy is not analyzed, despite being central to the claimed low-supervision paradigm.

Performance on the bounding-box stage does not generalize well to structurally complex data (Arcade drops to ~41%), and while this is acknowledged, it somewhat undercuts the narrative of steadily increasing localization capability from VQA to bbox to segmentation.

Comparison to fully specialized segmentation models (e.g., nnU-Net) is only qualitatively acknowledged as a gap rather than quantitatively benchmarked, leaving the practical clinical utility of RAU's absolute segmentation quality somewhat unclear.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and clinically relevant task formulation: reference-based anatomical understanding, which sidesteps the annotation scarcity problem by leveraging a small set of labeled reference images rather than requiring large-scale supervised datasets for every new structure/task.

Comprehensive multi-stage experimental design spanning VQA, bounding-box prediction, and pixel-level segmentation (VLM+SAM2), with each stage motivating the next based on observed limitations (e.g., bounding boxes failing on thin/curved vessels).

Strong empirical gains are demonstrated consistently: large improvements over the vanilla Qwen2.5-VL baseline and several medical VLM baselines (HuatuoGPT-Vision, Lingshu, Med-VLM-R1, MedFlamingo, MedRegA, BiRD, MedPLIB) in VQA labeling accuracy, and substantial Dice/gIoU improvements over SAM2/MedSAM2 memory baselines and reasoning-segmentation baselines (LISA, SegZero).

Good breadth of OOD evaluation across modalities (CT, X-ray, ultrasound, MRI), which is important for demonstrating the claimed generalization benefit of the reference-based spatial reasoning paradigm.

Thoughtful ablation studies, including VLM initialization (Vanilla vs SFT vs RL), reference quality stratified by LPIPS distance, and a spatial-shuffling control that specifically tests whether the model relies on spatial correspondence rather than semantic pattern matching—this is a nice sanity check supporting the core claim.
A practical annotation-efficiency study (Appendix C.6) quantifying real-world time/click savings, which strengthens the applied significance of the work beyond benchmark numbers.
Reasonably detailed implementation/hyperparameter documentation in the supplementary material aiding partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is largely a combination of existing components (GRPO/LoRA fine-tuning, SAM2 memory mechanism, DINOv2-based retrieval, optimal transport matching) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the novelty lies mainly in the task setting and integration, which is acknowledged in the text but somewhat overstated as a core contribution.

The pipeline depends on a curated reference bank matched via DINOv2 cosine similarity; the LPIPS-stratified ablation shows accuracy drops meaningfully when reference and target are dissimilar (e.g., 0.6-1.0 bin), raising concerns about robustness/practicality when a good reference is not available, which is a realistic clinical scenario not deeply analyzed.

Some OOD test sets are quite small (LERA has only 87 images, CAMUS 900), and no variance/error bars or multiple-run statistics are reported anywhere in the paper, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of reported gains.

The comparison against baselines such as Med-VLM-R1, MedFlamingo, HuatuoGPT-Vision, Lingshu, MedRegA, BiRD, and MedPLIB appears to be zero-shot/out-of-box rather than fine-tuned on the same reference-based task, which may understate their potential performance and makes the comparison somewhat unfair to those baselines.

Details on how continuous segmentation outputs are converted into discrete "labeling accuracy" (Table 2/4) are not clearly specified, creating ambiguity about this metric's definition and reproducibility.

The reward for bounding-box RL (Eq. 5) uses AP as a reward term, which is non-differentiable/coarse for typical GRPO advantage estimation; the paper does not clarify how this is handled in practice (likely fine given GRPO doesn't need differentiable rewards, but this should be clarified).

No public code or data release is mentioned, and given the complexity of the pipeline (multi-stage SFT/RL, custom reward shaping, retrieval infrastructure, cost-matrix construction), reproducibility could be challenging without released artifacts.

The RAOS dataset construction (450k training instances from only 413 patient scans via cross-patient slice matching) raises potential concerns about information leakage or over-representation of certain patients across train/test splits, which is not explicitly addressed.

Failure case analysis is relegated to the supplementary material and is fairly brief; a more systematic characterization of when/why the method fails (e.g., near-duplicate anatomical structures, severe misalignment) would strengthen the paper's claims about robustness.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: reference-based anatomical understanding under label scarcity, motivated clearly by real clinical annotation workflows (comparing target scans to reference images).

Comprehensive, staged experimental design (VQA → bbox → segmentation) that builds a coherent narrative for why finer-grained output representations are needed, with each stage empirically justified before moving to the next.

Strong quantitative results: substantial and consistent improvements over a wide range of relevant baselines (SAM2/MedSAM2 variants, LISA, SegZero, several medical VLMs such as HuatuoGPT-Vision, Lingshu, Med-VLM-R1, MedFlamingo) across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution datasets spanning CT, X-ray, and ultrasound.

Thoughtful ablations: the up-down split-and-shuffled reference experiment is a compelling sanity check that isolates spatial correspondence from semantic pattern matching, and the VLM-initialization ablation (Vanilla vs SFT vs RL) clarifies the contribution of the RL stage to OOD generalization.
Practical annotation-efficiency study (Appendix C.6) grounds the method's value in realistic time/click savings, strengthening the case for clinical relevance beyond benchmark numbers.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, LoRA configuration, dataset construction pipeline) provided in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the core building blocks (GRPO/RL fine-tuning, LoRA, SAM2 memory-based segmentation, <Seg> token grounding as in LISA) are largely adapted from existing techniques rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the contribution is more of a well-executed integration/task formulation than a new algorithm.

The DINOv2-based reference retrieval/template matching module (Fig. 2a) that selects the reference image at test time is not evaluated in isolation—its failure modes, sensitivity to reference bank size/coverage, and impact on end-to-end accuracy are not clearly separated from the VLM+SAM2 contribution.

Some OOD evaluation sets are quite small (e.g., LERA with 87 images, CAMUS with 900 images from 500 patients), and no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-run statistics are reported, making it hard to assess the robustness of the reported gains.

The 'labeling accuracy' metric used for the segmentation-integrated method (Table 2/3) is not fully and precisely defined for the segmentation output, making it somewhat difficult to compare directly across the VQA, bbox, and segmentation settings.

The optimal-transport-based global matching (Eq. 4) assumes an equal number of predicted boxes and label prototypes (N×N cost matrix), which seems to implicitly require knowing the number of targets in advance; this assumption and its practical handling (partial matches, missing/extra structures) are not clearly discussed in the main text.

No direct comparison to strong classical/foundation segmentation baselines (e.g., nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator) is provided for absolute context, only against SAM2/MedSAM2 variants and reasoning-based VLM segmenters, which limits understanding of how RAU compares to standard fully-supervised pipelines when ample labels exist.

Minor presentation issues remain (e.g., an unresolved placeholder 'Z,000' in the LERA dataset description in the supplementary material), suggesting the manuscript could benefit from another proofreading pass.
